title: Carved birch butter pat
subtitle: Seasoned birch: a ridged paddle for shaping butter curls
excerpt: A butter pat is a small ridged paddle used to shape softened butter into logs, rounds, and curls. Made from seasoned birch, which is food-safe, odourless, and close-grained enough to take a clean ridge pattern. The ridges are cut with a V-shaped chisel and refined with a detail knife.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (1885) for the hand-tool ridge-cutting method on small treen pieces; Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861) for butter-pat dimensions and use.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small domestic objects made entirely from wood, spoons, cups, bowls, paddles, and platters. The word comes from the Old English for 'of a tree'.
The rough-shaped piece of wood before detailed carving begins.

content.text: A butter pat is a flat ridged paddle used to roll and shape softened butter. Birch is the standard
treen

for dairy use: it is food-safe, takes no flavour from the wood into the butter, and its close grain holds a clean ridge line without chipping. The finished size is roughly 22 cm long, 5 cm wide at the paddle face, and 1 cm thick at the centre. Two pats used together roll butter into a cylinder; one alone can curl butter off a block.

This project uses seasoned birch, moisture content 8, 12% for indoor use. A birch board from a timber merchant works; so does kiln-dried birch from a woodcraft supplier. The grain needs to run along the length of the paddle for strength across the thin section.
Before you start cutting.
Grip: four-finger grip on the work; thumb-push grip on the knife. Never make a cut whose blade-path can reach a body part.
Cut direction: push cuts (blade away from body) and thumb-pivot cuts are the default. Pull cuts only with the work braced against the chest and the blade-arc unable to reach anything vital.
Sharpening: a dull tool is more dangerous than a sharp one, the dull tool slips. Strop every fifteen minutes of carving, hone weekly, oilstone monthly.
First aid: keep a styptic pencil, gauze, and a clean dressing within reach. Apply firm pressure, elevate, and dress. A cut that shows fat or won't close with pressure goes to A&E, not a plaster.
Workspace: stable seat, good light, no children or pets within arm-and-blade reach.
What you need
Wood

One piece of seasoned birch, 24 cm long, 6 cm wide, 1.5 cm thick. The grain must run along the length. Birch is pale, food-safe, and closes-grained enough to take sharp ridge lines. Maple or sycamore are direct alternatives with the same working properties. Avoid pine and any resinous softwood for food-contact dairy pieces.
Tools
Tenon saw for cutting the blank to length and the handle shoulder.
Sloyd knife for shaping the handle and chamfering the paddle face edges.
Detail knife for cutting the ridges.
120-grit and 240-grit sandpaper.
Board butter for finishing.
Workspace

A bench with a vice or clamp, or a low carving stool. The ridge-cutting is fine work, good direct light from above is important. A magnifier lamp is helpful if your eyes are not accustomed to close work.
The work
Step 1: Cut the blank and mark the profile
Cut the
blank

to 22 cm with the tenon saw. Mark the handle: the handle is 8 cm long and 2.5 cm wide, cut from the same thickness as the paddle face but narrower. The paddle face is the remaining 14 cm, the full 5 cm width. Draw a shoulder line at 14 cm from the paddle tip.
Step 2: Shape the handle
Use the tenon saw to cut the waste from the handle sides, down to the shoulder line. Then use the sloyd knife with
push cuts
to round the handle edges and taper the handle slightly toward the end. The junction between handle and paddle face is a clean right-angle shoulder on the face side; make a
stop cut
across the grain at this shoulder before cutting toward it from the handle.
Step 3: Chamfer the paddle face edges

Use push cuts to chamfer the four long edges of the paddle face, a 2 mm bevel at 45 degrees on each. This prevents the sharp edge splitting off in use. Sand the paddle face with 120-grit paper on a flat block, then 240-grit, until smooth.
Step 4: Mark and cut the ridges

Mark parallel lines across the paddle face at 4 mm intervals, running across the grain (perpendicular to the handle). These will become the ridges. With the detail knife, cut a V-groove along each line: first a stop cut straight down the line to a depth of about 1 mm, then a second angled cut from one side to meet it and lift a small chip. Repeat from the other side of the groove to produce a clean V. Work along the grain direction for the angled cuts, the grain runs the length of the paddle, so cuts perpendicular to the grain need care; make the stop cut first and do not try to pry the chip with the blade tip.
Step 5: Final sand and check

Run 240-grit sandpaper across the paddle face at an angle to the ridges to clean the tops of the ridges and leave them sharp. Do not sand along the ridge direction or you will round them off. Check the face is flat by sighting along it.
Finishing

Apply board butter (beeswax and food-grade mineral oil paste) to all surfaces. Work it into the grooves with a cloth. Leave for twenty minutes, then buff off the surplus. Board butter is not a curing finish, it re-coats often, roughly monthly. It is ready for food contact immediately after the first application dries.
Variations
Diamond pattern: mark two sets of parallel lines at 45 degrees to each other, then cut all the V-grooves. This gives a diamond grid on the paddle face, traditional on Victorian butter pats.
Wider paddle: increase the paddle face to 7 cm wide and 18 cm long for shaping a larger block of butter.
Maple version: maple is harder than birch and takes sharper ridge lines; it is the traditional Canadian alternative.
Care
Rinse in cold water after butter use. Never soak. Re-apply board butter when the wood looks dry. Do not put in a dishwasher.

attrs.symptom: Ridge chips out when the V-groove is cut
attrs.cause: Cutting against the grain on the angled side of the groove
attrs.fix: Always make the stop cut first, then the angled cut from each side. On a perpendicular-to-grain groove, work in from each side rather than across the full width in one pass.

attrs.symptom: The paddle face is not flat after shaping
attrs.cause: The handle shaping removed material unevenly from the back
attrs.fix: Use a flat sanding block (not folded paper) for the paddle face. Flatten the face first before adding the ridges.
